title: Cunda's meal
hookLine: the smith Cunda serves a last meal; the Buddha falls ill and makes sure Cunda is not blamed (DN 16)

cards: A cook stays up all night over one meal for a guest he admires. In the morning the guest sits down and eats. That night the guest falls terribly ill.
It's hard to think of a heavier thing to carry. In the town of Pava, a metalworker named Cunda hears that the Buddha is staying in his mango grove.
Cunda goes, listens to him teach, and invites him and the monks to a meal at his home the next day. He spends the night preparing good food. In the morning the Buddha comes, sits, and eats.
That meal turns out to be his last.

teach.h: NOBODY KNOWS WHAT THE DISH WAS.
teach.b: Among the dishes is one called sukaramaddava, and plainly: nobody knows exactly what it was. Its parts mean pig and soft, or tender, and even that doesn't settle it. Some ancient commentators said tender pork.
Others said a kind of mushroom or truffle, the sort pigs root for. Others said bamboo shoots, or a special preparation. Buddhists and scholars still argue, and the text leaves it open.
What the text does record is strange and careful.
The Buddha tells Cunda: serve that dish only to me. Give the others the rest of the food, and bury whatever is left of it in a pit. I see no one in the world who could digest it but me.
After the meal a severe illness comes on, with bleeding and sharp pains. The Buddha bears it, mindful and calm, and keeps walking toward Kusinara. On the road, he thinks of Cunda.
He tells Ananda: someone may make Cunda feel guilty. They'll say, it's your loss, friend Cunda, that the Buddha died after eating your food. If that happens, go to him.

Tell him two meals are equal in blessing, greater than all others: the meal the Buddha ate just before his awakening, and the meal he ate just before his final passing. Cunda's gift is one of those two.
In pain, near the end, his mind turns to a man who might blame himself, and he arranges comfort in advance. Not a word about fault. Only: this was a great gift.

how: Buddhists remember Cunda's meal as one of the two most blessed offerings of food, alongside Sujata's rice before the awakening, and the story is often told to show the Buddha's care for others' feelings even in his final illness.

games.q: you're gravely ill after a meal a kind man cooked for you. you know people will blame him. what do you do?
o: say nothing. it isn't your concern.
send word that his meal was one of the most blessed ever given.
warn others not to eat his food.
games.why: he tells Ananda to comfort Cunda: two meals are equal in blessing, the one before the awakening and the one before the final passing.

practice: Think of someone who might be blaming themselves for something that went wrong: a friend whose plan fell through, a coworker who made an honest mistake, a parent, maybe you. Picture them and the weight they carry.
Then think of one thing you could say, the way the Buddha sent word to Cunda, that would lift a little of it.

wordCard.voice: Cunda's meal. The last meal, offered by a smith in Pava. The Buddha fell ill, and made sure Cunda would never be blamed.

orig.note: Pali: the dish at the last meal. Sukara (pig) and maddava (soft, tender). What it was is unknown.

carryVoice: Your line: no one is to blame. Even in pain, his thoughts went to the cook. That's day eighty-one.
